questions.stem: A brachial plexus with a major contribution from C4 is described in the lecture as which variant?
questions.explanation: The lecture calls the plexus prefixed when it has a major C4 contribution; a major T2 contribution is termed postfixed.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 50 states that a prefixed plexus has a major C4 contribution and a postfixed plexus a major T2 contribution.

questions.stem: Which nerve pierces pectoralis minor before supplying it and then continues to supply pectoralis major?
questions.explanation: The medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor, supplies it, and then supplies pectoralis major.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 62 describes the medial pectoral nerve leaving the axilla by piercing pectoralis minor and supplying both pectoral muscles.

questions.stem: Which muscle is supplied by the lateral pectoral nerve according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lateral pectoral nerve is described as supplying pectoralis major only.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 63 says the lateral pectoral nerve arises from the lateral cord and supplies pectoralis major muscle only.

questions.topic: Cutaneous innervation of the upper limb
questions.stem: Which two nerves are exceptions to the brachial-plexus supply of upper-limb skin, as noted in the lecture?
options: Musculocutaneous and medial cutaneous nerves of forearm
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies skin above the deltoid and upper medial arm as supplied by the supraclavicular and intercostobrachial nerves, respectively.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 74 lists supraclavicular and intercostobrachial nerves as exceptions to brachial-plexus cutaneous supply.

questions.stem: In the cubital fossa, what structure separates the brachial artery from the median cubital vein?
questions.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis lies over the brachial artery and separates it from the median cubital vein.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 76 notes that the bicipital aponeurosis crosses the brachial artery and separates it from the median cubital vein.

questions.stem: Which pair forms the arterial anastomosis in front of the medial epicondyle?
options: Superior ulnar collateral and posterior ulnar recurrent arteries
Anterior branch of inferior ulnar collateral and anterior ulnar recurrent arteries
Radial recurrent and posterior descending profunda brachii arteries
Posterior ulnar recurrent and interosseous recurrent arteries
questions.explanation: The anterior branch of the inferior ulnar collateral artery joins the anterior ulnar recurrent artery in front of the medial epicondyle.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 80 lists the anterior branch of the inferior ulnar collateral and anterior ulnar recurrent arteries in front of the medial epicondyle.

questions.stem: At which landmark does the nutrient artery of the humerus enter the bone?
questions.explanation: The lecture places the humeral nutrient artery entry at the insertion of coracobrachialis.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 82 states that the nutrient artery enters the humerus at the insertion of coracobrachialis.

questions.stem: Which artery accompanies the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve travels in the spiral groove with the profunda brachii artery.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 82 says the profunda brachii accompanies the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus.

questions.stem: Moving from medial to lateral through the cubital fossa, which sequence of contents is correct?
options: Median nerve, brachial artery, bicipital tendon, radial nerve
Brachial artery, median nerve, radial nerve, bicipital tendon
Bicipital tendon, brachial artery, median nerve, radial nerve
Radial nerve, bicipital tendon, brachial artery, median nerve
questions.explanation: The listed order from medial to lateral is median nerve, brachial artery, bicipital tendon, and radial nerve.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 92 explicitly lists the cubital-fossa contents from medial to lateral, including median nerve then brachial artery; slide 93 completes the list with tendon and radial nerve.

questions.stem: How does the median nerve enter the forearm from the cubital fossa?
options: Between the two heads of pronator teres
Behind the medial epicondyle between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
Between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous
questions.explanation: The median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres as it leaves the cubital fossa.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 101 describes the median nerve leaving the cubital fossa between the two heads of pronator teres.

questions.stem: On which structure does the anterior interosseous nerve descend, and which artery accompanies it?
options: On the anterior surface of the interosseous membrane with the anterior interosseous artery
On the posterior surface of the ulna with the ulnar artery
Within the carpal tunnel with the radial artery
Along the posterior surface of the radius with the posterior interosseous artery
questions.explanation: The slide describes the anterior interosseous nerve descending on the front of the interosseous membrane with the anterior interosseous artery.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: The slide places the nerve on the anterior membrane surface and pairs it with the anterior interosseous artery.

questions.stem: At the wrist, how does the ulnar nerve enter the hand relative to the flexor retinaculum?
options: Deep to it through the carpal tunnel
Superficial to it, just lateral to the pisiform
Between the two heads of pronator teres
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes over the flexor retinaculum, just lateral to the pisiform, before dividing in the hand.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 109 states that the ulnar nerve enters over the flexor retinaculum just lateral to pisiform.

questions.stem: The deep terminal branch of the radial nerve becomes which nerve after piercing the supinator?
questions.explanation: The deep branch pierces the supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 114 identifies the deep branch of the radial nerve as the posterior interosseous nerve and describes its passage through supinator.

questions.stem: After crossing the anatomical snuffbox, through which interval does the radial artery enter the palm?
options: Between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous
Between the two heads of pronator teres
Between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
questions.explanation: The radial artery enters the palm between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 122 states that the radial artery enters the palm between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous, then continues as the deep palmar arch.

questions.stem: In the lower two-thirds of the forearm, what is the ulnar artery's position relative to the ulnar nerve?
options: Posterior to the ulnar nerve within the carpal tunnel
Superficial to the ulnar nerve in the anatomical snuffbox
questions.explanation: The ulnar artery descends lateral to the ulnar nerve in the lower two-thirds of the forearm.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 128 describes the artery in the lower two-thirds as deep to FCU, superficial to FDP, and lateral to the ulnar nerve.

questions.stem: Which artery contributes its descending carpal branch to the anterior carpal arch?
questions.explanation: The descending carpal branch of the anterior interosseous artery is one of the contributors to the anterior carpal arch.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.sourceEvidence: Slide 130 lists the descending carpal branch of the anterior interosseous artery among the anterior carpal arch contributors.
